units.title: How a type is built
units.blurb: What every object has: System.Object, the header and the type pointer, the Equals/GetHashCode contract; casts, is, as and unboxing; primitives, checked and overflow, dynamic and its cost.

lessons.title: System.Object inside out
lessons.sub: Six methods, the object header and the Equals/GetHashCode contract

cards.title: What every type inherits
cards.body:
Every type in .NET — class, struct, record, array — ultimately derives from System.Object. That is why every value has the same set of methods:

Public: Equals, GetHashCode, ToString — virtual, you can override them; GetType — not virtual.
Protected: MemberwiseClone — a shallow copy; Finalize — called by the garbage collector.
Static: ReferenceEquals and Equals(a, b).

cards.title: An object on the heap: two hidden words
cards.body:
When you write new Order(), the heap gets more than room for the fields. Two bookkeeping words sit in front of them:

The object header — bits for lock, the default hash code and a link to a sync block if one was needed.
The type pointer (MethodTable) — the address of the structure where the CLR keeps everything about the type: size, parent, interfaces, the virtual method table.

A reference in a variable points exactly at the type pointer. GetType, casts and virtual calls all work through it.
cards.deep:
On a 64-bit platform the header and the type pointer take 8 bytes each. The header sits at a negative offset: the reference points at the MethodTable word, and the header is 8 bytes before it. Even an empty class has a minimum object size of 24 bytes: the collector needs room for at least one pointer-sized field.

A struct on the stack or inside another object has neither word — just its fields. They appear when the struct is boxed: the box is an ordinary heap object with its own header and type pointer.

cards.q: How many bytes does an instance of an empty class Empty { } take on the heap in a 64-bit process?
cards.explain: 8 bytes of header, 8 bytes of type pointer and the minimum room for one pointer-sized field. On x64 no object is smaller than 24 bytes.

wrong.1: There are no fields, but every object has the bookkeeping words.
wrong.3: 16 is just the header and the type pointer. The CLR still reserves room for one more word.

cards.title: Why GetType cannot be overridden
cards.body:
GetType computes nothing: it takes the type pointer from the object itself and returns the matching Type. If the method were virtual, a class could lie: "I am a string." And all of type safety rests on that pointer telling the truth: casts, is, calling the right method.

So GetType is not virtual. You can hide it with new, but code that looks through object still gets the real type.
cards.deep:
The difference from typeof(T): typeof is the type known to the compiler, GetType() is the type of a particular object at run time. With Animal a = new Cat() the static type is Animal, but a.GetType() returns Cat.

A Nullable twist: int? x = 5; x.GetType() returns System.Int32. The call goes through boxing, and a boxed int? is simply a boxed int. If x is null, you get a NullReferenceException.

cards.q: Which System.Object methods can you override with override? Select all.
cards.explain: GetType and MemberwiseClone are not virtual. Finalize is virtual too, but in C# you write it with finalizer syntax ~Name() rather than override.

cards.title: How a dictionary finds a key
cards.body:
Dictionary and HashSet search in two steps: GetHashCode picks a bucket, and Equals compares against the entries in that bucket. Hence the contract:

1. If a.Equals(b), their hashes must match. The reverse is not required: equal hashes for different objects are an ordinary collision.
2. While an object is a dictionary key, its hash must not change.
3. Equals is reflexive, symmetric, transitive and returns false for null.

By default a class compares references in Equals, and GetHashCode is different for every object. Override only Equals and you break rule 1. The compiler warns you: CS0659.

cards.q: Point overrides only Equals. What does this code print?
cards.code:
var set = new HashSet<Point> { new Point { X = 1, Y = 2 } };
Console.WriteLine(set.Contains(new Point { X = 1, Y = 2 }));
cards.explain: Two different objects have different default hashes. The lookup goes to the wrong bucket (or is filtered out by the hash mismatch) and never reaches Equals. True is only possible on an accidental hash match.

wrong.3: CS0659 is a warning, not an error. The code builds and quietly works wrong.

cards.q: Point now overrides both Equals and GetHashCode using X and Y. Which line prints False?
cards.explain: After p.X = 10 the hash changed, but the object sits in the bucket computed from the old hash. The set looks in the new bucket and finds nothing — even though it is the very same object. Dictionary keys should be immutable.

cards.q: Complete the pair of methods so the contract holds
cards.explain: The pattern is Point p checks the type and rules out null at the same time. HashCode.Combine mixes the field hashes. Even simpler is a record: the compiler writes Equals and GetHashCode over all fields for you.

cards.title: MemberwiseClone and Finalize: what they cost
cards.body:
MemberwiseClone creates a new object of the same type and copies the fields bit by bit. No constructor runs, and reference fields are copied as references: the original and the copy share the same list. The method is protected — outside code cannot copy an object this way, only the type itself can.

Finalize is written in C# as ~Name(). It is not a destructor in the C++ sense: the garbage collector decides when it runs. Such an object is more expensive to create (it is registered in the finalization queue), and it survives an extra garbage collection.
cards.deep:
The compiler turns a finalizer into protected override void Finalize() that calls base.Finalize() in a finally. In modern .NET finalizers do not run at process exit (in .NET Framework they did), so you cannot rely on them even "at the very end". For resources use IDisposable and SafeHandle.

The with expression on records does not use MemberwiseClone: the compiler generates a copy constructor and a hidden clone method. The copy is still shallow.

cards.q: Match the method to what it does
pairs: Is it the very same object?
A shallow copy without a constructor

cards.q: What does object.ReferenceEquals(42, 42) return?
cards.explain: ReferenceEquals takes object, so each 42 is boxed into its own box. Two different boxes are two different references. For value types ReferenceEquals is always false.

lessons.title: Casts: is, as and patterns
lessons.sub: How the CLR checks a type, why (long)(object)42 fails and where operators stay silent

cards.title: Up is free, down is checked
cards.body:
A cast to a base type or an interface is implicit: the compiler already knows a Manager is an Employee. Nothing happens at run time; the reference stays the same.

Going back down to a derived type takes an explicit cast in parentheses. The compiler does not know what really sits in the variable, so it inserts a check that runs at run time.

The same parentheses do different things: for numbers, (int)3.9 is a conversion of the value (you get 3); for references, it is only a check of the type, and the object does not change.

cards.title: How the CLR checks a cast
cards.body:
For (Manager)o the compiler emits the IL instruction castclass. At run time the CLR reads the type pointer from the object and compares it with Manager. No match — it walks up the parent chain, and for an interface, through the type's list of interfaces. Found — the cast succeeds. Not found — InvalidCastException.

An important detail: null passes any cast to a reference type. There is nothing to check, so there is no exception.
cards.deep: In modern .NET this logic lives in managed code (the CastHelpers class in the runtime) and uses a cache of cast results. A cast to a sealed class is often reduced by the JIT to a single pointer comparison: there are no subclasses, so the type must match exactly. A cast to an interface or to a class deep in a hierarchy costs more. These are nanoseconds, but in a hot loop over millions of objects the difference shows up in a profiler.

cards.q: Manager derives from Employee. Which line throws InvalidCastException?
cards.explain: o holds an Employee, not a Manager: a parent does not become a subclass. The null line passes: casting null to a reference type always succeeds.

cards.title: is, as and patterns
cards.body:
is and as compile to the IL instruction isinst: the same check, but without an exception. is returns a bool, as returns the reference or null.

Older code often checks the type twice: first with is, then with a cast. The pattern is Manager m does one check and hands you a variable of the right type straight away.

cards.q: Match the expression to what happens when o is not a Manager
Why does int n = o as int; not compile?
options: as returns null on failure, and an int cannot be null
An int cannot be taken out of an object
You have to write as Int32
cards.explain: For value types write o as int? or, better, o is int n: the check and the unboxing in one step.

cards.title: is null and is not null
cards.body: A class can overload == — and then x == null calls its code, which may be wrong or slow. The patterns is null and is not null never call overloaded operators: the compiler compares the reference itself with null.

cards.title: Unboxing: the exact type only
cards.body:
A boxed int is a heap object whose type pointer says "Int32". Unboxing (IL unbox) checks that the box holds exactly the requested type and copies the value. It does no numeric conversion at all.

That is why (long)(object)42 fails with InvalidCastException, even though (long)42 works. Unbox to the exact type first, then convert.
cards.code:
object o = 42;          // the box holds Int32
long a = (long)o;       // InvalidCastException
long b = (long)(int)o;  // unbox the int, then widen
int c = (int)(object)null!; // NullReferenceException
cards.deep: The "exactly the same type" rule has exceptions. An enum and its underlying integer type unbox into each other: (DayOfWeek)(object)1 works. A boxed int can be unboxed into int?, and a boxed int? does not exist at all: boxing turns a Nullable into either a box with an int or null. Unboxing null into int gives a NullReferenceException, into int? simply null.

cards.q: object o = 42; Which expression runs without an exception?
cards.explain: The box can only be unboxed into Int32. After that, (long) is an ordinary widening numeric conversion.

cards.title: Conversion operators are invisible through object
cards.body:
A user-defined explicit operator is a static method. The compiler picks it based on static types: from Celsius to Fahrenheit, it calls the operator. But if the value sits in an object, the compiler sees "object → Fahrenheit" and emits a plain unbox. At run time the box holds a Celsius, not a Fahrenheit — InvalidCastException.

The same scenario breaks code during a refactoring: a parameter changes from Celsius to object, everything compiles, and the cast starts failing.

cards.q: Which lines throw InvalidCastException? Select all.
options: object o = new Celsius(5); var f = (Fahrenheit)o;
cards.explain: A string is not an int; unboxing needs the exact type; a conversion operator is not called through object. null passes a cast to string, and an int unboxes fine from a box holding an int.

cards.q: Complete the pattern checks
cards.code:
if (o is ___ m) m.Approve();

if (input is not ___) Use(input);
cards.explain: is Manager m is a type check and a variable in one step. is not null checks the reference without any overloaded !=.

lessons.title: Primitives, checked and dynamic
lessons.sub: int is System.Int32, overflow is silent by default, and dynamic pays on every call

cards.title: int is just another name
cards.body:
C# keywords are aliases for library types: int is System.Int32, long is System.Int64, string is System.String, object is System.Object. A compiled assembly has no "int" in it — only Int32.

The size does not depend on the platform: an int is always 32 bits. The exception is nint and nuint: these are pointer-sized integers, 32 bits in a 32-bit process and 64 in a 64-bit one.
cards.code:
int a = 5;
System.Int32 b = a;        // the same type, not a conversion
Console.WriteLine(a.GetType());   // System.Int32

nint p = 0;                // System.IntPtr
Console.WriteLine(IntPtr.Size);   // 8 in a 64-bit process
cards.deep: nint and nuint arrived in C# 9 as separate keywords on top of IntPtr/UIntPtr, with arithmetic. Since C# 11 and .NET 7 they are full aliases: nint and IntPtr are the same thing, operators included. They are for interop and low-level code: indexes into native memory, buffer lengths, offsets.

cards.q: Match the C# keyword to the CLR type

cards.title: What "primitive" means to the CLR
cards.body:
To the CLR, a primitive is a type that has its own IL instructions. Adding two ints is the add instruction, and the JIT turns it into a single machine instruction.

decimal looks the same — it has literals like 1.5m and operators. But to the CLR it is an ordinary 16-byte struct. For decimal, a + b compiles to a call to the op_Addition method, and the arithmetic is done in software. That is why decimal is noticeably slower than double — you pay for an exact decimal fraction.
cards.code:
int x = a + b;       // IL: add
double y = c + d;    // IL: add
decimal z = m + n;   // IL: call Decimal.op_Addition
cards.deep: Type.IsPrimitive returns true for Boolean, Byte, SByte, Int16, UInt16, Int32, UInt32, Int64, UInt64, IntPtr, UIntPtr, Char, Single and Double. For decimal and string it returns false. A const decimal is allowed in C#, but the metadata does not store it as an ordinary literal constant — it uses the DecimalConstantAttribute attribute instead.

cards.q: What does typeof(decimal).IsPrimitive return?
cards.explain: decimal has no IL instructions of its own: its operators are ordinary static methods of the Decimal struct.

cards.title: Overflow is silent by default
cards.body:
For integers the compiler emits the add instruction by default. It does not check for overflow: the high bits are simply dropped. int.MaxValue + 1 gives int.MinValue — no exception.

In a checked context the compiler emits add.ovf, and overflow throws OverflowException. The same goes for an explicit narrowing: (int)someLong cuts off the high bits when unchecked and throws when checked.

The cost of the check is a compare and a conditional jump after the operation. Usually that is pennies, but in tight loops it can get in the way of JIT optimizations.

cards.q: A project with default settings. Which line throws OverflowException?
cards.explain: The default context is unchecked: a becomes int.MinValue, and b gets the low 32 bits (705032704). The exception only happens where checked is written explicitly.

cards.title: Constants, the project flag and where checked ends
cards.body:
Constants are evaluated by the compiler itself and are always checked: int x = int.MaxValue + 1; is error CS0220. When overflow is intended (in a hash function, say), write unchecked(...).

The project flag <CheckForOverflowUnderflow>true</CheckForOverflowUnderflow> makes checked the default context for the whole project. It is often turned on in Debug to catch overflows during tests.

Boundaries: checked only affects code written inside the block. Methods called from there are compiled by their own rules.

Other numbers: decimal always throws OverflowException, double and float never throw — they go to infinity.
cards.code:
int x = int.MaxValue + 1;             // error CS0220
int y = unchecked(int.MaxValue + 1);  // allowed: -2147483648

checked { Helper(); }  // inside Helper — its own context
cards.deep: Since C# 11 a numeric type of your own can declare two versions of an operator: the regular one and operator checked +. The compiler calls the checked version in a checked context. That is how the built-in types in generic math work, for example Int128.

cards.q: What throws OverflowException without any checked? Select all.
cards.explain: decimal always checks for overflow, and so do the Convert methods. An int silently wraps when unchecked, and a double becomes infinity.

cards.title: dynamic: the type is resolved at run time
cards.body:
To the CLR, dynamic is object with a marker. The compiler does not check whether the value has the method; instead, at every operation it creates a call site — an object that picks the method at run time.

On the first call, the runtime binder from the Microsoft.CSharp assembly looks at the actual types of the arguments and finds the method using C# rules. It compiles the result into a rule — "if the types are these, call that" — and puts it in the call site cache. Later calls with the same types go straight through the ready rule.

No method found — RuntimeBinderException at run time, not a compile error.
cards.code:
dynamic d = "text";
int n = d.Length;   // 4: Length is found at run time
d = 42;             // the int is boxed: dynamic is object
d.Foo();            // RuntimeBinderException
cards.deep:
A call site is a CallSite<T> with a Target delegate. The cache has several levels: the rule in the delegate itself, a set of recent rules for this call site and a shared binder cache. If one place receives a string one time and a List the next, the rules multiply, and with frequently changing types the cost of the check grows too.

What dynamic cannot do: extension methods (the binder does not look for them), and lambdas as arguments without an explicit delegate type. It also does not get along well with trimming and Native AOT: the binder relies on reflection and on generating code at run time.

cards.q: Put in order what happens on the first call to d.Foo(1)
items: The compiler has already created a call site for this operation
The call site cache is empty — the call goes to the runtime binder
The binder looks at the actual types of d and the argument
It picks the Foo method using C# rules
It compiles a rule and puts it in the cache
The next call with the same types uses the cached rule
cards.explain: Only the first pass is expensive: binding and compiling the rule. After that it is a type check and a call through a delegate.

cards.q: dynamic d = new List<int>(); d.Sum(); — what happens?
cards.explain: Sum is an extension method from System.Linq. The binder only looks at the type's own methods, so it does not find it. This works: Enumerable.Sum((List<int>)d).

wrong.2: With dynamic the compiler checks nothing — the error only shows up at run time.

cards.q: What is true about the cost of dynamic? Select all.
options: The first call at each call site is expensive
Value types in dynamic are boxed
Type errors only show up at run time
After the first call it is as fast as a regular call
cards.explain: Even from the cache, the call goes through a delegate with a type check — slower than a direct call. dynamic fits COM, schemaless JSON and scripting, not hot code.

units.title: Generics
units.blurb: Why they exist, how the JIT compiles them for value and reference types, where constraints, covariance and contravariance, and generic math with INumber<T>.

lessons.title: Why generics
lessons.sub: One piece of code for many types — no object, no casts

cards.title: Life before generics
cards.body: In .NET 1.0, collections stored object. You could put anything in, but getting it out took a cast. Make a mistake and you found out at run time.
cards.code:
var list = new ArrayList();
list.Add(42);           // int is boxed into object
list.Add("forty-two");  // a string is fine too
int x = (int)list[1];   // InvalidCastException at run time

cards.q: Which line fails at run time?
cards.explain: The second element is a string, and the cast to int is only checked at run time.

cards.title: List<T>: the type is a parameter
cards.body: A generic is code with a type parameter T. The compiler plugs in a concrete type and checks everything up front. Value types are not boxed: List<int> stores real ints.

cards.task: Max must compare a and b and work with both int and string. Add the constraint it needs.

cards.q: Why can't you call a.CompareTo(b) without a constraint?
options: Nothing is known about T — an arbitrary type may not have CompareTo
You have to cast to object first
cards.explain: A constraint is a promise to the compiler: "T has this."

cards.title: How the JIT compiles generics
cards.body: For all reference types the JIT emits one shared piece of machine code: a reference is always 8 bytes. Each value type gets its own: List<int> and List<double> each get separate, fast code with no boxing.

cards.q: How many machine-code versions of Add do List<string>, List<object> and List<int> get?
options: Two: one shared by string and object, one for int
cards.explain: Reference types share code; value types get their own.

cards.q: Match them up
What do generics give you? Select all.
options: Code that runs without the JIT
cards.explain: The JIT still compiles the code — just for specific types.

lessons.title: where constraints
lessons.sub: class, struct, new(), unmanaged and interfaces

cards.title: What you can require of T
cards.body:
class — a reference type (can be null).
struct — a value type.
unmanaged — a value type with no references inside (works with stackalloc and pointers).
new() — has a public parameterless constructor.
An interface — T has its methods.

cards.task: A factory creates a new object of type T. It must work with List<int> and Point.

cards.q: Why doesn't string satisfy new()?
options: string has no public parameterless constructor
cards.explain: new string() does not compile — so string does not satisfy new() either.

cards.task: A cache holds a T value and can reset it to null. It must work with string and List<int>, but not with int.
A fast stack buffer via stackalloc. It must work with int and Point.

cards.title: What doesn't mix
cards.body: class and struct can't be combined. unmanaged already means "value type", so you don't write it with struct, class or new(). Order: class/struct/unmanaged first, then interfaces, new() last.

cards.q: Order of constraints
cards.code: T Make<T>() where T : ___, IDisposable, ___
cards.explain: new() always goes at the end of the list.

cards.q: What does default(T) return for T = int and T = string?
cards.explain: default means "zeros": the zero value for value types, null for reference types.

cards.q: Match the constraint to what it allows
Which types satisfy where T : struct? Select all.
cards.explain: string is a reference type. int? is Nullable<int>: it is a value type, but the struct constraint deliberately rejects it.

lessons.title: Variance and generic math
lessons.sub: out T, in T and INumber<T>

cards.title: Why List<string> is not a List<object>
cards.body: If that assignment were allowed, you could put a number into a list of strings through the "list of objects" — and break it.
cards.code:
List<object> objs = new List<string>();   // compile error
objs.Add(42);                              // and this is why

cards.title: Covariance: out T
cards.body: IEnumerable<T>, on the other hand, only hands out T and never takes one in. So a sequence of strings can safely be treated as a sequence of objects. That is marked with out: IEnumerable<out T>.
cards.code: IEnumerable<object> objs = new List<string> { "a", "b" };   // allowed

cards.title: Contravariance: in T
cards.body: Action<in T> only takes in T. An action that can print any object also works where an action for string is expected.
cards.code:
Action<object> print = o => Console.WriteLine(o);
Action<string> printText = print;   // allowed

cards.q: Which assignment compiles?
cards.explain: IList takes elements in (Add), so it is invariant.

cards.q: Match them up

cards.title: The array trap
cards.body: Arrays have been covariant since .NET 1.0 — before generics existed. The compiler lets this through, and it fails at run time:
cards.code:
object[] arr = new string[2];
arr[0] = 42;   // ArrayTypeMismatchException

cards.title: Generic math (C# 11, .NET 7)
cards.body: You used to be unable to write Sum<T> for any number type: T has no + operator. Now interfaces can require static members, and INumber<T> gives you +, −, Zero and the rest.

cards.q: A sum for any number type
cards.explain: Zero is a static property from the interface, so you write T.Zero.

cards.q: Why does the compiler accept object[] arr = new string[2], even though it is risky?
options: Array covariance stayed from .NET 1.0 for compatibility; the check happens at run time
cards.explain: Generic interfaces made variance safe, but arrays stayed as they were.

lessons.title: Final: generics
lessons.sub: Constraints, the JIT and variance

cards.task: The method creates a T and compares values. It must work with int, and must reject string.

cards.q: where T : struct, new() — what does the compiler say?
options: Error: a struct always has a parameterless constructor, so new() is not allowed with it
cards.explain: With struct, new T() is already allowed.

cards.q: You pass an IEnumerable<Cat> where an IEnumerable<Animal> is expected. Does it work?
cards.explain: Covariance works for reference types in interfaces and delegates.

cards.q: Which are true? Select all.
options: For reference-type T the JIT emits shared code
object[] arr = new string[1]; arr[0] = 1; fails at run time
cards.explain: string is a reference type, so it is not unmanaged.

cards.q: Match the task to the constraint
Which line will not compile?
cards.explain: An unconstrained T cannot be null — T might be int. default always works.

cards.q: The constraint that allows T x = null
cards.code: class Box<T> where T : ___
cards.explain: Only reference types (and Nullable<T>) can be null.

cards.q: Why did C# 11 add static abstract interface members?
options: So a generic can require operators and static properties — like + and Zero on numbers
cards.explain: INumber<T> and all of generic math are built on this.

units.title: Delegates, events and closures
units.blurb: Func and Action, multicast delegates, events and subscription leaks, lambdas and exactly what they capture.

lessons.title: Delegates and lambdas
lessons.sub: A method as a value

cards.title: A variable that holds a method
cards.body: A delegate is an object that holds a reference to a method. You can pass it to another method, put it in a list, or call it later.

cards.title: Func, Action, Predicate
cards.body:
Func<…, TResult> — takes arguments and returns a result (the last type parameter is the result type).
Action<…> — returns nothing.
Predicate<T> — returns bool.

cards.q: Match the signature to the delegate

cards.title: A lambda is a method without a name
cards.body: You can write a method right where you need it: x => x * 2. The compiler infers the types from where the lambda is passed.
cards.code:
var evens = numbers.Where(x => x % 2 == 0);
Func<int, int> twice = x => x * 2;

cards.q: A delegate that takes a string and returns bool
cards.code: ___<string, ___> isEmpty = s => s.Length == 0;
cards.explain: Predicate<string> would work too, but there are two gaps here — Func<string, bool>.

cards.title: One delegate, several methods
cards.body: Delegates are multicast: += adds a method to the invocation list. Calling the delegate runs them all in order. If it returns a value, you get the result of the last one.

cards.q: What does this code print?
cards.explain: Both run, but you get the result of the last one in the list.

cards.q: How is Action different from Func?
options: Action returns nothing, Func returns a result
cards.explain: Func<int> returns an int; Action<int> takes an int and returns nothing.

cards.q: Which are true about delegates? Select all.
options: A delegate is an object on the heap
You can pass a delegate to a method
+= adds a method to the invocation list
A lambda cannot be a delegate
cards.explain: A lambda is exactly what turns into a delegate (or an expression tree).

lessons.title: Events
lessons.sub: A delegate outsiders can only subscribe to

cards.title: Why the event keyword
cards.body:
A public delegate field is dangerous: anyone can invoke it or wipe out every subscriber with =.

event leaves outsiders only += and -=. Only the owning class can raise the event.

cards.q: Which line will not compile outside the Button class?
cards.explain: From the outside an event only has += and -=. You cannot assign or invoke it.

cards.q: Why the ?. in Clicked?.Invoke(...)?
options: With no subscribers the event is null — without ?. you get a NullReferenceException
cards.explain: An event with no subscribers is null.

cards.title: The standard shape
cards.body: By convention a handler receives the sender and the arguments: EventHandler<TArgs>.
cards.code:
public event EventHandler<OrderEventArgs>? OrderPlaced;

shop.OrderPlaced += (sender, e) => Console.WriteLine(e.OrderId);

cards.title: A subscription holds on to the subscriber
cards.body: The publisher stores the delegate, and the delegate stores a reference to the subscriber object. As long as the publisher is alive and you have not unsubscribed, the garbage collector will not collect the subscriber. The classic leak: a window subscribes to a global event and never unsubscribes.

cards.q: A window subscribed to the static event App.ThemeChanged and closed without unsubscribing. What happens?
options: The window stays in memory: the event holds a reference to it
The garbage collector collects the window
The event unsubscribes the closed window by itself
cards.explain: More on this in ".NET under the hood", in the "Garbage collection and resources" unit.

cards.q: Raise the event only if there are subscribers
cards.code: Clicked___Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty);
cards.explain: A null-conditional call.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Raise only if there are subscribers
Unsubscribe and let the object go

cards.q: Which are true? Select all.
options: Only the owning class can raise an event
An event with no subscribers is null
A subscription keeps the subscriber in memory
Outsiders can clear an event with =
cards.explain: Blocking = from the outside is exactly what event is for.

lessons.title: Closures
lessons.sub: A lambda captures the variable, not the value

cards.title: A lambda sees outer variables
cards.body: A lambda can use the variables of the method it was created in. So the variable can outlive the method, the compiler moves it into a hidden object on the heap, and the lambda holds a reference to that object.

cards.task: Three lambdas are created in a for loop. Step through: what will they print?

cards.q: Why did all three lambdas print 3?
options: They captured the same variable i, and by the time they ran it was 3
cards.explain: The variable is captured, not its value at the moment the lambda was created.

cards.task: Fix it: make it print 0 1 2, but keep the for loop.
And how does foreach behave?

cards.q: What does this code print?
cards.explain: The lambda changes the very same count variable — it now lives in the hidden object.

cards.title: foreach was fixed in C# 5
cards.body: Before C# 5, foreach had the same trap. It was fixed: the foreach variable is now fresh on every iteration. Not so with for: there really is one variable for the whole loop.

cards.title: The cost of capturing
cards.body: Capturing means a heap object plus a delegate. In hot code that runs millions of times, that is extra work for the GC. The static keyword in front of a lambda (C# 9) forbids capturing — the compiler checks that the lambda pulls nothing from outside.
cards.code: var r = items.Where(static x => x > 0);   // captures nothing

cards.q: What does static do in front of x => x > limit, where limit is a local variable?
options: Compile error: a static lambda cannot capture limit
cards.explain: static guarantees there is no capture.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: int j = i inside the loop

lessons.title: Final: delegates and closures
lessons.sub: Methods as values

cards.task: Get the output 0 1 2 any way you like.

cards.q: What does this code print?
cards.explain: The lambda reads the variable at the moment it is called.

cards.q: Where is the memory leak?
cards.explain: Subscribing to a static event without unsubscribing keeps the window in memory forever.

cards.q: Match them up
What does a lambda that captures a local variable create? Select all.
options: A hidden object for the variable
A copy of the variable on the stack
cards.explain: The variable moves into an object on the heap, and the lambda becomes a delegate.

cards.q: What does a multicast Func<int> made of two methods return?
options: The result of the last one
cards.explain: To get them all, loop over GetInvocationList().

cards.q: Unsubscribe when the window closes
cards.code: App.ThemeChanged ___ OnThemeChanged;
cards.explain: Once you unsubscribe, the event stops holding on to the window.

cards.q: Why does for have the closure trap while foreach does not?
options: Since C# 5 the foreach variable is fresh on each iteration, while for has one for the whole loop
cards.explain: The C# 5 change was technically breaking, but everyone saw it as a fix.

units.title: LINQ and its cost
units.blurb: Deferred execution and Take, ToList and multiple enumeration, the buffering OrderBy, IQueryable and SQL from lambdas.

lessons.title: Lazy LINQ
lessons.sub: A query is a recipe, not a result

cards.title: Describing ≠ running
cards.body: The line var q = numbers.Where(…).Select(…) computes nothing. It only builds a chain. The work starts when something enumerates the result: foreach, ToList, Count, First…

cards.task: Step through the query. Watch the order in which Where and Select are called and where the query stops.

cards.q: Why were only four of the six numbers read?
options: Take(2) got two elements and stopped asking for more
cards.explain: The chain pulls elements one at a time. Once it has enough, it stops pulling.

cards.q: In what order do the calls happen?
options: Each element goes through the whole chain before the next is taken: Where(1), Where(5), Select(5)…
Where for all of them first, then Select for all
cards.explain: This is what streaming means.

cards.title: Trap: the data changed
cards.body: Since the query runs when it is enumerated, it sees the data as of enumeration, not as of when you wrote it.

cards.q: What does this code print?
cards.explain: 2, 3 and 10 — the query ran after the Add.

cards.q: What triggers the query to run? Select all.
cards.explain: Where and Select only add links to the chain.

cards.q: Match them up

lessons.title: ToList and multiple enumeration
lessons.sub: When to store the result, and when not to

cards.title: Every enumeration starts over
cards.body: A query does not remember its result. Enumerate it twice and the whole chain runs twice: reading again, Where again, Select again. If the source is a database or a file, that is two trips to it.

cards.task: The query is enumerated twice: Count() and foreach. Make the source read at most 6 times in total.

cards.q: With ToList, why is the source read only once even though it is still enumerated twice?
options: ToList ran the chain once and stored a list; Count() and foreach work on that list
cards.explain: Once materialized, you enumerate the list, not the query.

cards.task: Here ToList is unnecessary: because of it, Where runs for all six numbers. Get Where down to at most 4 calls.

cards.q: With ToList before Take, why did Where run 6 times?
options: ToList needs every element, so Take can no longer stop the reading
cards.explain: ToList is a wall: everything before it runs to completion.

cards.title: The rule
cards.body:
Materialize (ToList, ToArray) if the result is enumerated several times or the source is expensive.
Don't materialize if you enumerate once or a Take/First comes later — laziness saves work.

The IDE warns you: "Possible multiple enumeration".

cards.q: Where does the database query run a second time?
cards.explain: Any() ran the query, and foreach runs it again. If you need all the users, call ToList() right away.

cards.q: When should you call ToList()? Select all.
options: The result is enumerated several times
The source is a slow database or file, and you need the result later
You need to freeze the data before the source changes
cards.explain: Before First(), ToList only forces reading everything.

cards.q: Match them up

lessons.title: The cost of LINQ, and IQueryable
lessons.sub: Buffering, allocations and SQL from lambdas

cards.title: Not every operator streams
cards.body: To hand out the first element, OrderBy has to see them all — the smallest one might be last. Operators like this buffer: OrderBy, GroupBy, Reverse, Distinct (partly).

cards.task: Add OrderBy before Where and step to the end. How many numbers have to be read?

cards.q: Take(2) comes after OrderBy. Does Take save you from reading every element?
options: No: OrderBy reads and sorts everything before handing out the first one
Only if there is little data
cards.explain: Sorting is a buffering operation.

cards.title: Where LINQ costs you
cards.body:
Every capturing lambda is an object; every operator has its own enumerator. In everyday code this does not matter. In a hot loop that spins millions of times a second (a game, a server under load), a plain for loop can be several times faster.

LINQ gets faster with every .NET release — profile first, rewrite second.

cards.q: What is faster for checking "is there at least one element"?
options: Any() — stops at the first one
cards.explain: For a list Count is cheap, but for a query or a database Any() does not scan everything.

cards.title: IQueryable: a lambda becomes SQL
cards.body: In Entity Framework, queries are IQueryable. A lambda there is not compiled into a method; it becomes an expression tree that EF translates into SQL.
cards.code:
db.Users.Where(u => u.Age > 18).Select(u => u.Name)
// SELECT Name FROM Users WHERE Age > 18

cards.q: Inside an EF Where you call your own C# method IsVip(u), which SQL knows nothing about. What happens in EF Core?
options: An exception: the expression cannot be translated to SQL
EF quietly loads the whole table
The method runs on the database server
cards.explain: Since EF Core 3.0, untranslatable expressions are no longer run quietly in memory — EF fails loudly.

cards.q: After which line does filtering happen in memory instead of in the database?
cards.code:
var names = db.Orders
    .Where(o => o.Total > 100)
    .AsEnumerable()
    .Where(o => IsVip(o.Customer))
    .Select(o => o.Id);
cards.explain: AsEnumerable switches to LINQ to Objects: from there on everything runs in C#, and the database sends every order over 100.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: The lambda is a regular method
The lambda is an expression tree

cards.q: Which are true? Select all.
options: EF Core translates Where lambdas into SQL
AsEnumerable moves the rest of the work into memory
LINQ is always 100 times slower than for
cards.explain: There is a difference, but it is usually small and matters only on hot paths.

lessons.title: Final: LINQ
lessons.sub: Laziness, materialization and SQL

cards.task: The query is enumerated twice, and an extra OrderBy gets in the way. Make the source read at most 6 times and Where run at most 6 times.

cards.q: How many times does the query run?
cards.explain: Count, First and ToList each run the chain from scratch.

cards.q: What does OrderBy do when Take(1) follows it?
options: Reads and sorts everything, then hands out one
cards.explain: For the minimum, Min() or MinBy() is better — one pass, no sorting.

cards.q: Which line pulls extra data from the database?
cards.code:
var vip = db.Customers
    .ToList()
    .Where(c => c.Total > 1000)
    .Take(10);
cards.explain: ToList loaded every customer into memory, so the filter and Take ran in C#.

cards.q: Which of these run the query? Select all.
cards.explain: OrderBy and Where only describe steps.

cards.q: Match the symptom to the cause
Check for a match without scanning everything
cards.code: if (orders.___(o => o.IsLate)) Warn();
cards.explain: Any with a condition stops at the first match.

cards.q: When is it worth rewriting LINQ as a loop?
options: When the profiler shows a hot path with LINQ and its allocations
cards.explain: Measure first, optimize second.

units.title: Performance
units.blurb: Span<T> and copy-free slices, the rules of ref struct and Memory<T>, readonly struct, in and defensive copies.

lessons.title: Span<T>
lessons.sub: A window into memory, no copying

cards.title: A window, not a copy
cards.body: Span<T> is a "window" into a chunk of memory: a start and a length. The memory can be an array, a string, the stack or a native buffer. A slice span[2..5] copies nothing — it is a new window onto the same bytes.

cards.q: What is in arr[1] after middle[0] = 20?
options: 20 — the Span looks at the same array
cards.explain: A Span does not own memory; it just looks at it.

cards.task: Parsing the string "12,34,56" creates garbage right now. Pick a way that puts not a single object on the heap.

cards.q: Why does Split create 4 objects for the string "12,34,56"?
options: An array for the parts plus three new strings
cards.explain: Strings are immutable, so every part is a new string.

cards.title: ReadOnlySpan<char> and the stack
cards.body:
You can view a string as a ReadOnlySpan<char>: slices without copies, and int.Parse can read straight from a slice.

A small temporary buffer can live on the stack — no heap at all:
cards.code:
Span<byte> buf = stackalloc byte[256];
int written = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("hello", buf);

cards.q: Slice a string without copying
cards.code:
ReadOnlySpan<char> s = line.___();
var head = s[..___];
cards.explain: Substring would create a new string.

cards.q: Match them up
What can a Span look at? Select all.
cards.explain: Native memory too. A file has to be read into a buffer first.

cards.q: Why bother, if the GC cleans up garbage anyway?
options: Less garbage means fewer collections and pauses; in hot code the difference is huge
The GC cannot clean up strings
cards.explain: The fastest object is the one you never created.

lessons.title: ref struct: the rules of Span
lessons.sub: Why a Span can't be a field or cross an await

cards.title: A Span lives only on the stack
cards.body: A Span can point into stack memory. If a Span ended up on the heap, it would outlive its method — and point into a stack that now belongs to someone else. That is why Span is a ref struct: the compiler won't let it reach the heap.

cards.title: What you can't do
cards.body:
You can't store a Span in a class field, box it (into object or an interface), capture it in a lambda, or hold it across await or yield.

Since C# 13 you can declare a Span in an async method — but only between awaits, not across them.

cards.q: Which line will not compile?
cards.explain: A class field lives on the heap, and a Span is not allowed there.

cards.q: Where is the error?
cards.explain: head is used after the await — so it would have to survive the suspension and move to the heap. Not allowed.

cards.title: Memory<T> — for the heap and async
cards.body: Need a window you can store in a field or pass across an await? Use Memory<T>: a regular struct that can live anywhere, and .Span gives you a Span for work right here, right now.

cards.q: You need to keep a slice of a buffer in a class field. What do you choose?
cards.explain: Memory<T> is a regular struct with none of the ref struct restrictions.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Fine in a field and across await
Get a Span from a Memory

cards.q: What can't you do with a Span<T>? Select all.
options: Store it in a class field
Pass it as a parameter to a regular method
cards.explain: Passing it as a parameter is fine — that is still the stack.

lessons.title: readonly struct and in
lessons.sub: Defensive copies you can't see in the code

cards.title: A struct is copied whole
cards.body:
Pass a struct to a method and it gets copied. For a small one (int, Point) that is cheap. A 4×4 matrix is already 64 bytes on every call.

ref and in pass a reference instead of a copy. in also promises that the method won't change the struct.

cards.task: Get rid of the matrix copies, but make sure the method can't mess up the caller's matrix.

cards.q: Why did copies remain with in but without readonly struct?
options: The compiler doesn't know whether Det() and Trace() change the struct, so it calls them on a copy to keep the in promise
cards.explain: That is a defensive copy: invisible, but real.

cards.task: This one already uses in, yet there are two copies per call. Remove them without changing how the matrix is passed.

cards.title: readonly struct
cards.body:
readonly struct promises that no method changes the fields. The compiler checks this and can then call methods directly on the original — even through in.

In a regular struct you can mark individual methods readonly.

cards.q: What is the danger of ref instead of in?
options: The method can change the caller's struct
cards.explain: ref is for when you actually want the change.

cards.q: Match the passing mode to its behavior
No copies and no changes
cards.code:
public ___ struct Vec4 { … }
float Len(___ Vec4 v) => …;
cards.explain: The pair that in was invented for.

cards.q: A Point struct holds two ints. Is it worth passing it with in?
options: Usually not: copying 8 bytes costs no more than passing a reference
cards.explain: in pays off for large structs — 16–32 bytes and up.

lessons.title: Final: performance
lessons.sub: Span, ref struct, copies

cards.task: Start with Substring and find a way with no allocations.
The method takes the matrix by ref. Make it safe and copy-free.

cards.q: What will not compile?
cards.explain: A ref struct cannot be boxed: an object lives on the heap.

cards.q: You need to pass a buffer to an async method that writes to a stream. What do you pass?
cards.explain: A Span cannot be held across an await.

cards.q: What reduces pressure on the GC? Select all.
cards.explain: ToList creates a new list — that is extra garbage.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: A window for the heap and async

cards.q: Why can't a Span be a field of a class?
options: It may point into the stack, and a class object outlives the method — the window would point at garbage
cards.explain: ref struct is how the compiler guarantees safety without run-time checks.

cards.q: in + a regular (non-readonly) struct with two method calls inside. How many defensive copies?
options: Two — one before each method call
cards.explain: Each method call on an in parameter is made on a copy.

units.title: Modern C#
units.blurb: Pattern matching, records, nullable references, required and what is new in C# 12, 13 and 14. The course final.

lessons.title: Pattern matching
lessons.sub: is, switch expressions and arm order

cards.title: Check and extract in one go
cards.body: is checks the type and declares a variable at the same time. Property patterns look inside the object.
cards.code:
if (shape is Circle { R: > 10 } big)
    Console.WriteLine($"big circle {big.R}");

cards.title: The switch expression
cards.body: Arms are checked top to bottom, and the first match wins. _ means "everything else", null included. The compiler complains (CS8510) if an arm can never be reached because everything is already caught above it.

cards.task: The arms are mixed up: a point becomes a circle, a square becomes a rectangle, and null becomes "something else". Put them in order with the ▲ buttons.

cards.q: Why did null end up in "something else"?
options: _ catches everything, null included, and the null arm was below it
You can't check for null in a switch
cards.explain: Specific cases go higher, general ones lower.

cards.title: More patterns
cards.body:
Relational: < 0, >= 18.
Logical: and, or, not.
List (C# 11): [1, .., var last].

cards.q: What does Grade(95) return?
cards.explain: 95 is neither below 0 nor above 100, but it is ≥ 90 — the first matching arm.

cards.q: Not null and not an empty string
cards.code: if (name is ___ null ___ "") Greet(name);
cards.explain: name is not null and not "" — it reads almost like plain English.

cards.q: Match the pattern to its meaning
The arm Rect r sits above Rect { W: var w, H: var h } when w == h. What does the compiler say?
options: CS8510: the second arm is unreachable — every Rect is already caught
It picks the more specific arm by itself
cards.explain: The compiler doesn't reorder arms — the first one wins.

lessons.title: Records
lessons.sub: Value equality and with

cards.title: A value type in one line
cards.body: A record (C# 9) is a class for which the compiler writes the constructor, properties, content-based equality, ToString and deconstruction for you.

cards.q: a and b are two different record Point(1, 2) objects. What does a == b return?
cards.explain: A regular class would give False — it would compare references.

cards.title: with: a copy with changes
cards.body: The properties of a positional record are init: they don't change after creation. Need a modified version? Make a copy.
cards.code: var moved = a with { X = 10 };   // Point { X = 10, Y = 2 }, a is unchanged

cards.q: Which line will not compile?
cards.explain: Age is an init property. You change it with with.

cards.title: record struct
cards.body: Since C# 10 there is record struct — a value type with the same conveniences. Its properties are mutable by default; readonly record struct makes them init.

cards.q: What does a record generate for you? Select all.
options: A ToString that shows the contents
cards.explain: Saving is the ORM's job, not the language's.

cards.q: Where do records shine?
options: DTOs, messages, dictionary keys, immutable values
EF entities with mutable state and identity
cards.explain: An entity with an Id is usually compared by Id, not by every field.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Value type with the same conveniences
Can only be set at creation

lessons.title: Nullable references
lessons.sub: string and string? are different promises

cards.title: The billion-dollar mistake
cards.body:
NullReferenceException is the most common error in .NET. Since C# 8 you can turn on the nullable context: then string means "never null here", and string? means "may be null". The compiler keeps track and warns you.

New projects have it on by default: <Nullable>enable</Nullable>.

cards.q: On which line does the compiler warn about a possible null?
cards.explain: CS8602: name may be null. Check it, or use name?.Length.

cards.title: Keeping the compiler happy, honestly
cards.body:
Check: if (name is not null) — after that the compiler knows it is not null.
A default value: name ?? "guest".
Last resort: name! — "trust me, it's not null". If you're wrong, you get that very exception.

cards.q: What does the ! operator do in name!.Length?
options: It only silences the warning; nothing is checked at run time
It checks for null and throws a clear exception
It turns null into an empty string
cards.explain: It exists only for the compiler.

cards.title: required
cards.body: A property can't be null, but it is set by an initializer rather than the constructor? required (C# 11) forces you to set it at creation.

cards.q: The name, or "guest" if it is null
cards.code: var shown = name ___ "guest";
cards.explain: The null-coalescing operator.

cards.q: Match them up
Which are true about nullable references? Select all.
options: It is a compiler check, not a runtime one
They are on by default in new projects
After if (x is not null) the compiler treats x as not null
cards.explain: Nullable<T> is only for value types. string? is just an annotation for the compiler.

lessons.title: C# 12, 13 and 14
lessons.sub: What the latest versions added

cards.title: C# 12: primary constructors
cards.body: Constructor parameters go right in the class header. Key point: these are not properties but parameters available throughout the class body.

cards.q: Given class Service(IRepo repo), can outside code write service.repo?
options: No: repo is a parameter, not a public property
cards.explain: In a record, positional parameters become properties; in a regular class they don't.

cards.title: C# 12: collection expressions
cards.body: Square brackets create an array, a list, a Span — whatever the target type needs. .. spreads another collection in.

cards.q: A list of zero, the elements of a, and five
cards.code: List<int> all = [0, ___a, 5];
cards.explain: The spread is two dots.

cards.title: C# 13
cards.body:
params collections: params ReadOnlySpan<int> instead of an array — no allocation.
A new lock type, System.Threading.Lock (.NET 9): lock on it is faster than on an object.
ref struct in async methods — between awaits.
cards.code:
private readonly Lock _gate = new();

lock (_gate) { _count++; }

cards.title: C# 14 (.NET 10)
cards.body:
field — the hidden backing field of an auto-property.
extension blocks — extension properties, not just methods.
?.= — assign only if the left side is not null.
Implicit Span conversions: an array turns into a Span by itself wherever one is expected.
cards.code:
public string Title { get; set => field = value.Trim(); }

order?.Status = Status.Paid;

cards.q: Match the feature to the version
What does order?.Status = Status.Paid do if order == null?
cards.explain: Null-conditional assignment, new in C# 14.

cards.q: What arrived in C# 12–14? Select all.
cards.explain: async is from C# 5, LINQ from C# 3.

lessons.title: Course final
lessons.sub: Everything together

cards.task: Fix the switch: every shape should land in its own arm.
The method puts T into a stack buffer and sorts it. It must accept int.
Make it print 0 1 2 while keeping the for loop.

cards.q: How many times does the query run?
cards.code:
var q = users.Where(u => u.IsActive);
if (q.Any()) Console.WriteLine(q.Count());
cards.explain: Any and Count are two separate enumerations.

cards.q: Where is the compile error?
cards.explain: The properties of a positional record are init-only.

cards.q: Match the task to the tool
pairs: Parse a string with no garbage
A big struct with no copies
A sum for any number type

cards.q: What does the compiler check, rather than the runtime? Select all.
options: Going out of a Span's bounds
cards.explain: Span bounds are checked at run time — IndexOutOfRangeException.

cards.q: Why can't a List<string> be assigned to a List<object>, while an IEnumerable<string> can go into an IEnumerable<object>?
options: IEnumerable only hands out elements (out T), but you could put a foreign type into a List
cards.explain: Variance is about type safety.

cards.q: A property that trims whitespace, in C# 14
cards.code: public string Name { get; set => ___ = value.Trim(); }
cards.explain: this.Name would recurse forever.
